{{Short description|Theorem about fixed points of multiple variables}}
In [[computability theory]], '''Bekić's theorem''' or '''Bekić's lemma''' is a [[fixed-point theorem|theorem about fixed-points]] which allows splitting a mutual recursion into recursions on one variable at a time.<ref name=Winskel>{{cite book |last1=Winskel |first1=Glynn |title=The Formal Semantics of Programming Languages: An Introduction |date=5 February 1993 |publisher=MIT Press |isbn=978-0-262-73103-4 |page=163 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JzUNn6uUxm0C&pg=PA163 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Díaz-Caro |first1=Alejandro |last2=Martínez López |first2=Pablo E. |title=Proceedings of the 27th Symposium on the Implementation and Application of Functional Programming Languages |chapter=Isomorphisms considered as equalities: Projecting functions and enhancing partial application through an implementation of λ <sup>+</sup> |date=2015 |pages=8 |doi=10.1145/2897336.2897346|arxiv=1511.09324|isbn=978-1-4503-4273-5 |s2cid=10413161 }}</ref><ref name="harper">{{cite web |last1=Harper |first1=Robert |title=Tarski's Fixed Point Theorem for Power Sets|work=15-819 Computational Type Theory Notes |date=Spring 2020 |url=http://www.cs.cmu.edu/~rwh/courses/chtt/pdfs/tarski.pdf |access-date=7 March 2022}}</ref> It was created by Austrian Hans Bekić (1936-1982) in 1969,<ref name="Bekic">{{cite book |last1=Bekić |first1=Hans |title=Programming Languages and Their Definition |chapter=Definable operations in general algebras, and the theory of automata and flowcharts |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |date=1984 |volume=177 |pages=30–55 |doi=10.1007/BFb0048939|isbn=3-540-13378-X }}</ref> and published posthumously in a book by [[Cliff Jones (computer scientist)|Cliff Jones]] in 1984.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Jones|first1=Cliff B. |editor-first1=C. B |editor-last1=Jones |title=Programming Languages and Their Definition |date=1984 |volume=177 |doi=10.1007/BFb0048933 |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/bfm%3A978-3-540-38933-0%2F1.pdf|chapter=Front matter|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |isbn=3-540-13378-X |s2cid=7488558 }}</ref>

The theorem is set up as follows.<ref name="Winskel"/><ref name="Bekic"/> Consider two operators <math>f : P \times Q \to P</math> and <math>g : P \times Q \to Q</math> on [[complete partial order|pointed directed-complete partial order]]s <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math>, [[Scott continuity|continuous]] in each component. Then define the operator <math>(f, g)(x, y) = (f (x, y), g(x, y))</math>. This is monotone with respect to the [[product order]] (componentwise order). By the [[Kleene fixed-point theorem]], it has a least fixed point <math>\mu (x, y).(f, g)(x, y)</math>, a pair <math>(x_0, y_0)</math> in <math>P \times Q</math> such that <math>f (x_0, y_0) = x_0</math> and <math>g(x_0, y_0) = y_0</math>.

Bekić's theorem (called the "bisection lemma" in his notes)<ref name="Bekic"/> is that the simultaneous least fixed point <math>\mu (x, y).(f, g)(x, y)</math> can be separated into a series of least fixed points on <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math>, in particular the fixed point is equal to <math>(x_0,y_0)</math> as follows:

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
x_0 &= \mu x . f ( x , \mu y . g(x,y) ) \\
y_0 &= \mu y . g ( x_0 , y )
\end{align}
</math>

In this presentation <math>y_0</math> is defined in terms of <math>x_0</math>. It can instead be defined in a symmetric presentation:<ref name="Winskel" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Leiss |first1=Hans |date=2016 |title=The Matrix Ring of a mu-Continuous Chomsky Algebra is mu-Continuous |url=https://drops.dagstuhl.de/opus/volltexte/2016/6546/pdf/LIPIcs-CSL-2016-6.pdf |journal=25th EACSL Annual Conference on Computer Science Logic (CSL 2016) |series=Leibniz International Proceedings in Informatics (LIPIcs) |volume=62 |pages=6:1–6:15 |doi=10.4230/LIPIcs.CSL.2016.6 |doi-access=free |isbn=9783959770224}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Arnold |first1=A. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MkWZaiECJvQC&pg=PA27 |title=Rudiments of Calculus |last2=Niwinski |first2=D. |date=7 February 2001 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-0-08-051645-5 |page=27 |language=en}}</ref>

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
x_0 &= \mu x . f ( x , \mu y . g(x,y) ) \\
y_0 &= \mu y . g ( \mu x . f(x,y), y )
\end{align}
</math>

'''Proof''' (Bekić):<ref name="Bekic"/>
:Taking <math>y_0 = \mu y . g ( x_0 , y )</math>, it is clear that <math>y_0 = g(x_0,y_0)</math> since <math>y_0</math> is the fixed point. Similarly letting <math>x_0 = \mu x . f ( x , \mu y . g(x,y) )</math>, we have <math>x_0 = f ( x_0 , \mu y . g(x_0,y) ) = f(x_0,y_0)</math>. Hence <math>(x_0,y_0)</math> is a fixed point of <math>(f,g)</math>.
:Furthermore, if there is a pre-fixed point <math>(x_1,y_1)</math> with <math>(x_1,y_1) \geq (f(x_1,y_1),g(x_1,y_1))</math>, then <math>x_1 \geq f ( x_1 , \mu y . g(x_1,y)) \geq x_0</math> and <math>y_1 \geq \mu y . g ( x_1 , y ) \geq \mu y . g ( x_0 , y ) = y_0</math>; hence <math>(x_1,y_1) \geq (x_0,y_0)</math> and we conclude <math>(x_0,y_0)</math> is the minimal fixed point.

== Variants ==

=== In a complete lattice ===
A variant of the theorem strengthens the conditions on <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math> to be that they are [[complete lattice]]s, and finds the [[least fixed point]] using the [[Knaster–Tarski theorem]]. The requirement for continuity of <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> can then be weakened to only requiring them to be [[monotonic function]]s.<ref name="Winskel" /><ref name="harper" />

=== Categorical formulation ===
Bekić's lemma has been generalized to fix-points of endofunctors of categories (initial [[F-algebra|<math>F</math>-algebras]]).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lehmann |first1=Daniel J. |last2=Smyth |first2=Michael B. |date=1981-12-01 |title=Algebraic specification of data types: A synthetic approach |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01752392 |journal=Mathematical Systems Theory |language=en |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=97–139 |doi=10.1007/BF01752392 |s2cid=23076697 |issn=1433-0490|url-access=subscription }} Theorem 4.2.</ref>

Given two functors <math>F : \mathbf{C} \times \mathbf{D} \to \mathbf{C}</math> and <math>G : \mathbf{C} \times \mathbf{D} \to \mathbf{D}</math> such that all <math>\mu X.F(X,Y)</math> and <math>\mu Y.G(X,Y)</math> exist, the fix-point <math>\mu \langle X,Y\rangle .\langle F(X,Y),G(X,Y)\rangle </math> is carried by the pair:

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
X_0 &= \mu X . F ( X , \mu Y . G(X,Y) ) \\
Y_0 &= \mu Y . G ( X_0 , Y )
\end{align}
</math>

== Usage ==

Bekić's theorem can be applied repeatedly to find the least fixed point of a [[tuple]] in terms of least fixed points of single variables. Although the resulting expression might become rather complex, it can be easier to reason about fixed points of single variables when designing an [[automated theorem prover]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Andersen |first1=Henrik Reif |last2=Winskel |first2=Glynn |title=Computer Aided Verification |chapter=Compositional checking of satisfaction |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |date=1992 |volume=575 |pages=24–36 |doi=10.1007/3-540-55179-4_4|isbn=978-3-540-55179-9 |doi-access=free}}</ref>
